entries.1c926984b71326a9a13997bf69f48ec4d60949ae: <div sID="gen6527" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="2" osisID="1Kgs.2" sID="1Kgs.2"/> <div eID="gen6527" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6528" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen6529" type="x-p"/> In this chapter we have David setting and Solomon at the same time rising. I. The conclusion of David's reign with his life. 1. The charge he gives to Solomon upon his death-bed, in general, to serve God (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.2.1-1Kgs.2.4">ver. 1-4</reference>), in particular, concerning Joab, Barzillai, and Shimei, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.2.5-1Kgs.2.9">ver. 5-9</reference>. 2. His death and burial, and the years of his reign, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.2.10-1Kgs.2.11">ver. 10, 11</reference>. II. The beginning of Solomon's reign, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.2.12">ver. 12</reference>. Though he was to be a prince of peace, he began his reign with some remarkable acts of justice, 1. Upon Adonijah, whom he put to death for his aspiring pretensions, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.2.13-1Kgs.2.25">ver. 13-25</reference>. 2. Upon Abiathar, whom he deposed from the high priesthood for siding with Adonijah, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.2.26-1Kgs.2.27">ver. 26, 27</reference>. 3. Upon Joab, who he put to death for his late treasons and former murders, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.2.28-1Kgs.2.35">ver. 28-35</reference>. 4. Upon Shimei, whom, for cursing David, he confined to Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.2.36-1Kgs.2.38">ver. 36-38</reference>), and three years after, for transgressing the rules, put to death, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.2.39-1Kgs.2.46">ver. 39-46</reference>.
entries.7edf227a32ec98e7fca4a5e659ce45f4f5f55e8c: <div eID="gen6529" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen6528" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">David's Dying Charge; David's Death and Burial. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1015.)</title> <div sID="gen6530" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Now the days of David drew nigh that he should die; and he charged Solomon his son, saying, <hi type="super">2</hi> I go the way of all the earth: be thou strong therefore, and show thyself a man; <hi type="super">3</hi> And keep the charge of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thy God, to walk in his ways, to keep his statutes, and his commandments, and his judgments, and his testimonies, as it is written in the law of Moses, that thou mayest prosper in all that thou doest, and whithersoever thou turnest thyself: <hi type="super">4</hi> That the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> may continue his word which he spake concerning me, saying, If thy children take heed to their way, to walk before me in truth with all their heart and with all their soul, there shall not fail thee (said he) a man on the throne of Israel. <hi type="super">5</hi> Moreover thou knowest also what Joab the son of Zeruiah did to me, <hi type="italic">and</hi> what he did to the two captains of the hosts of Israel, unto Abner the son of Ner, and unto Amasa the son of Jether, whom he slew, and shed the blood of war in peace, and put the blood of war upon his girdle that <hi type="italic">was</hi> about his loins, and in his shoes that <hi type="italic">were</hi> on his feet. <hi type="super">6</hi> Do therefore according to thy wisdom, and let not his hoar head go down to the grave in peace. <hi type="super">7</hi> But show kindness unto the sons of Barzillai the Gileadite, and let them be of those that eat at thy table: for so they came to me when I fled because of Absalom thy brother. <hi type="super">8</hi> And, behold, <hi type="italic">thou hast</hi> with thee Shimei the son of Gera, a Benjamite of Bahurim, which cursed me with a grievous curse in the day when I went to Mahanaim: but he came down to meet me at Jordan, and I sware to him by the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , saying, I will not put thee to death with the sword. <hi type="super">9</hi> Now therefore hold him not guiltless: for thou <hi type="italic">art</hi> a wise man, and knowest what thou oughtest to do unto him; but his hoar head bring thou down to the grave with blood. <hi type="super">10</hi> So David slept with his fathers, and was buried in the city of David. <hi type="super">11</hi> And the days that David reigned over Israel <hi type="italic">were</hi> forty years: seven years reigned he in Hebron, and thirty and three years reigned he in Jerusalem. <div eID="gen6530" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6531" type="x-p"/> David, that great and good man, is here a dying man (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.2.1">v. 1</reference>), and a dead man, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.2.10">v. 10</reference>. It is well there is another life after this, for death stains all the glory of this, and lays it in the dust. We have here, <div eID="gen6531" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6532" type="x-p"/> I. The charge and instructions which David, when he was dying, gave to Solomon, his son and declared successor. He feels himself declining, and is not backward to own it, nor afraid to hear or speak of dying: <hi type="italic">I go the way of all the earth,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Kgs.2.2">v. 2</reference>. Heb. <hi type="italic">I am walking in it.</hi> Note, Death is a way; not only a period of this life, but a passage to a better. It is <hi type="italic">the way of all the earth,</hi> of all mankind who dwell on earth, and are themselves earth, and therefore must return to their earth. Even the sons and heirs of heaven must <hi type="italic">go the way of all the earth,</hi> they must needs die; but they walk with pleasure in this way, <hi type="italic">through the valley of the shadow of death,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.23.4">Ps. xxiii. 4</reference>. Prophets, and even kings, must go this way to brighter light and honour than prophecy or sovereignty. David is going this way, and therefore gives Solomon directions what to do. <div eID="gen6532" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6533" type="x-p"/> 1. He charges him, in general, to keep God's commandments and to make conscience of his duty, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.2.2-1Kgs.2.4">v. 2-4</reference>. He prescribes to him, (1.) A good rule to act by—the divine will: "Govern thyself by that." David's charge to him is to <hi type="italic">keep the charge of the Lord</hi> his <hi type="italic">God.</hi> The authority of a dying father is much, but nothing to that of a living God. There are great trusts which we are charged with by the Lord our God—let us keep them carefully, as those that must give account; and excellent statutes, which we must be ruled by—let us also keep them. The written word is our rule. Solomon must himself do <hi type="italic">as was written in the law of Moses.</hi> (2.) A good spirit to act with: Be <hi type="italic">strong and show thyself a man,</hi> though in years but a child. Those that would keep the charge of the Lord their God must put on resolution. (3.) Good reasons for all this. This would effectually conduce, [1.] To the prosperity of his kingdom. It is the way to <hi type="italic">prosper in all thou doest,</hi> and to succeed with honour and satisfaction in every undertaking. [2.] To the perpetuity of it: <hi type="italic">That the Lord may continue</hi> and so confirm <hi type="italic">his word which he spoke concerning me.</hi> Those that rightly value the treasure of the promise, that sacred <hi type="italic">depositum,</hi> cannot but be solicitous to preserve the entail of it, and very desirous that those who come after them may do nothing to cut it off. Let each, in his own age, successively, keep God's charge, and then God will be sure to continue his word. We never let fall the promise till we let fall the precept. God had promised David that the Messiah should come from his loins, and that promise was absolute: but the promise that there should not fail him <hi type="italic">a man on the throne of Israel</hi> was conditional—if his seed behave themselves as they should. If Solomon, in his day, fulfil the condition, he does his part towards the perpetuating of the promise. The condition is that he walk before God in all his institutions, in sincerity, with zeal and resolution; and, in order hereunto, that he <hi type="italic">take heed to his way.</hi> In order to our constancy in religion, nothing is more necessary than caution and circumspection. <div eID="gen6533" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6534" type="x-p"/> 2. He gives him directions concerning some particular persons, what to do with them, that he might make up his deficiencies in justice to some and kindness to others. (1.) Concerning Joab, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.2.5">v. 5</reference>. David was now conscious to himself that he had not done well to spare him, when he had made himself once again obnoxious to the law, but the murder of Abner first and afterwards of Amasa, both of them great men, <hi type="italic">captains of the hosts of Israel.</hi> He slew them treacherously (<hi type="italic">shed the blood of war in peace</hi>), and injuriously to David: <hi type="italic">Thou knowest what</hi> he <hi type="italic">did to me</hi> therein. The murder of a subject is a wrong to the prince, it is a loss to him, and is against the peace of our sovereign lord the king. These murders were particularly against David, reflecting upon his reputation, he being, at that time, in treaty with the victims, and hazarded his interest, which they were very capable of serving. Magistrates are the avengers of the blood of those they have the charge of. It aggravated Joab's crime that he was neither ashamed of the sin nor afraid of the punishment, but daringly wore the girdle and shoes that were stained with innocent blood, in defiance of the justice both of God and the king. David refers him to Solomon's wisdom (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.2.6">v. 6</reference>), with an intimation that he left him to his justice. Say not, "He has a hoary head; it is a pity it should be cut off, for it will shortly fall of itself." No, let it not <hi type="italic">go down to the grave in peace.</hi> Though he has been long reprieved, he shall be reckoned with at last; time does not wear out the guilt of any sin, particularly that of murder. (2.) Concerning Barzillai's family, to whom he orders him to be kind for Barzillai's sake, who, we may suppose, by this time, was dead, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.2.7">v. 7</reference>. When David, upon his death-bed, was remembering the injuries that had been done, he could not forget the kindnesses that had been shown, but leaves it as a charge upon his son to return them. Note, the kindnesses we have received from our friends must not be buried either in their graves or ours, but our children must return them to theirs. Hence, perhaps, Solomon fetched that rule (<reference osisRef="Prov.27.10">Prov. xxvii. 10</reference>), <hi type="italic">Thy own friend, and thy father's friend, forsake not.</hi> Paul prays for the house of Onesiphorus, who had often refreshed him. (3.) Concerning Shimei, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.2.8-1Kgs.2.9">v. 8, 9</reference>. [1.] His crime is remembered: <hi type="italic">He cursed me with a grievous curse;</hi> the more grievous because he insulted him when he was in misery and poured vinegar into his wounds. The Jews say that one thing which made this a grievous curse was that, besides all that is mentioned (<reference osisRef="2Sam.16.1-2Sam.16.23">2 Sam. xvi.</reference>), Shimei upbraided him with his descent from Ruth the Moabitess. [2.] His pardon is not forgotten. David owned he had sworn to him that he would not himself put him to death, because he seasonably submitted, and cried <hi type="italic">Peccavi—I have sinned,</hi> and he was not willing, especially at that juncture, to use the sword of public justice for the avenging of wrongs done to himself. But, [3.] His case, as it now stands, is left with Solomon, as one that knew what was fit to be done and would do as he found occasion. David intimates to him that his pardon was not designed to be perpetual, but only a reprieve for David's life: "<hi type="italic">Hold him not guiltless;</hi> do not think him any true friend to thee or thy government, nor fit to be trusted. He has no less malice than he had then, though he has more sense to conceal it. He is still a debtor to the public justice for what he did then; and, though I promised him that I would not put him to death, I never promised that my successor should not. His turbulent spirit will soon give thee an occasion, which thou shouldst not fail to take, for the bringing of his <hi type="italic">hoary head to the grave with blood.</hi>" This proceeded not from personal revenge, but a prudent zeal for the honour of the government and the covenant God had made with his family, the contempt of which ought not to go unpunished. Even a hoary head, if a guilty and forfeited head, ought not to be any man's protection from justice. <hi type="italic">The sinner, being a hundred years old, shall be accursed,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.65.20">Isa. lxv. 20</reference>. <div eID="gen6534" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6535" type="x-p"/> II. David's death and burial (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.2.10">v. 10</reference>): He <hi type="italic">was buried in the city of David,</hi> not in the burying place of his father, as Saul was, but in his own city, which he was the founder of. There were set the thrones, and there the tombs, of the house of David. Now <hi type="italic">David, after he had served his own generation, by the will of God, fell asleep, and was laid to his fathers, and saw corruption,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.13.36">Acts xiii. 36</reference>, and see <reference osisRef="Acts.2.29">Acts ii. 29</reference>. His epitaph may be taken from <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.1">2 Sam. xxiii. 1</reference>. Here lies <hi type="italic">David the son of Jesse, the man who was raised up on high, the anointed of the God of Jacob, and the sweet psalmist of Israel,</hi> adding his own words (<reference osisRef="Ps.16.9">Ps. xvi. 9</reference>), <hi type="italic">My flesh also shall rest in hope.</hi> Josephus says that, besides the usual magnificence with which his son Solomon buried him, he put into his sepulchre a vast deal of money; and that 1300 years after (so he reckons) it was opened by Hircanus the high priest, in the time of Antiochus, and 3000 talents were taken out for the public service. The years of his reign are here computed (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.2.11">v. 11</reference>) to be forty years; the odd six months which he reigned above seven years in Hebron are not reckoned, but the even sum only.
entries.fbf6ee4f1f027d6304813c816687a26efc123cb5: <div eID="gen6535" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Adonijah's Impudent Request; Adonijah Put to Death. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1015.)</title> <div sID="gen6536" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">12</hi> Then sat Solomon upon the throne of David his father; and his kingdom was established greatly. <hi type="super">13</hi> And Adonijah the son of Haggith came to Bathsheba the mother of Solomon. And she said, Comest thou peaceably? And he said, Peaceably. <hi type="super">14</hi> He said moreover, I have somewhat to say unto thee. And she said, Say on. <hi type="super">15</hi> And he said, Thou knowest that the kingdom was mine, and <hi type="italic">that</hi> all Israel set their faces on me, that I should reign: howbeit the kingdom is turned about, and is become my brother's: for it was his from the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">16</hi> And now I ask one petition of thee, deny me not. And she said unto him, Say on. <hi type="super">17</hi> And he said, Speak, I pray thee, unto Solomon the king, (for he will not say thee nay,) that he give me Abishag the Shunammite to wife. <hi type="super">18</hi> And Bathsheba said, Well; I will speak for thee unto the king. <hi type="super">19</hi> Bathsheba therefore went unto king Solomon, to speak unto him for Adonijah. And the king rose up to meet her, and bowed himself unto her, and sat down on his throne, and caused a seat to be set for the king's mother; and she sat on his right hand. <hi type="super">20</hi> Then she said, I desire one small petition of thee; <hi type="italic">I pray thee,</hi> say me not nay. And the king said unto her, Ask on, my mother: for I will not say thee nay. <hi type="super">21</hi> And she said, Let Abishag the Shunammite be given to Adonijah thy brother to wife. <hi type="super">22</hi> And king Solomon answered and said unto his mother, And why dost thou ask Abishag the Shunammite for Adonijah? ask for him the kingdom also; for he <hi type="italic">is</hi> mine elder brother; even for him, and for Abiathar the priest, and for Joab the son of Zeruiah. <hi type="super">23</hi> Then king Solomon sware by the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , saying, God do so to me, and more also, if Adonijah have not spoken this word against his own life. <hi type="super">24</hi> Now therefore, <hi type="italic">as</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> liveth, which hath established me, and set me on the throne of David my father, and who hath made me a house, as he promised, Adonijah shall be put to death this day. <hi type="super">25</hi> And king Solomon sent by the hand of Benaiah the son of Jehoiada; and he fell upon him that he died. <div eID="gen6536" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6537" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. Solomon's accession to the throne, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.2.12">v. 12</reference>. He came to it much more easily and peaceably than David did, and much sooner saw his government established. It is happy for a kingdom when the end of one good reign is the beginning of another, as it was here. <div eID="gen6537" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6538" type="x-p"/> II. His just and necessary removal of Adonijah his rival, in order to the establishment of his throne. Adonijah had made some bold pretensions to the crown, but was soon obliged to let them fail and throw himself upon Solomon's mercy, who dismissed him upon his good behaviour, and, had he been easy, he might have been safe. But here we have him betraying himself into the hands of Solomon's justice, and falling by it, the righteous God leaving him to himself, that he might be punished for his former treason and that Solomon's throne might be established. Many thus ruin themselves, because they know not when they are well off, or well done to; and sinners, by presuming on God's patience, treasure up wrath to themselves. Now observe, <div eID="gen6538" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6539" type="x-p"/> 1. Adonijah's treasonable project, which was to marry Abishag, David's concubine, not because he was in love with her, but because, by her, he hoped to renew his claim to the crown, which might stand him in stead, or because it was then looked upon as a branch of the government to have <hi type="italic">the wives of the predecessor,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Sam.12.8">2 Sam. xii. 8</reference>. Absalom thought his pretensions much supported by lying with his father's concubines. Adonijah flatters himself that if he may succeed him in his bed, especially with the best of his wives, he may by that means step up to succeed him in his throne. Restless and turbulent spirits reach high. It was but a small game to play at, as it should seem, yet he hoped to make it an after-game for the kingdom, and now to gain that by a wife which he could not gain by force. <div eID="gen6539" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6540" type="x-p"/> 2. The means he used to compass this. He durst not make suit to Abishag immediately (he knew she was at Solomon's disposal, and he would justly resent it if his consent were not first obtained, as even Ishbosheth did, in a like case, <reference osisRef="2Sam.3.7">2 Sam. iii. 7</reference>), nor durst he himself apply immediately to Solomon, knowing that he lay under his displeasure; but he engaged Bathsheba to be his friend in this matter, who would be forward to believe it a matter of love, and not apt to suspect it a matter of policy. Bathsheba was surprised to see Adonijah in her apartment, and asked him if he did not come with a design to do her a mischief, because she had been instrumental to crush his late attempt. "No," says he, "I come <hi type="italic">peaceably</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.2.13">v. 13</reference>), and to beg a favour" (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.2.14">v. 14</reference>), that she would use the great interest she had in her son to gain his consent, that he might marry Abishag (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.2.16-1Kgs.2.17">v. 16, 17</reference>), and, if he may but obtain this, he will thankfully accept it, (1.) As a compensation for his loss of the kingdom. He insinuates (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.2.15">v. 15</reference>), "Thou knowest the kingdom was mine, as my father's eldest son, living at the time of his death, <hi type="italic">and all Israel set their faces on me.</hi>" This was false; they were but a few that he had on his side; yet thus he would represent himself as an object of compassion, that had been deprived of a crown, and therefore might well be gratified in a wife. If he may not inherit his father's throne, yet let him have something valuable that was his father's, to keep for his sake, and let it be Abishag. (2.) As his reward for his acquiescence in that loss. He owns Solomon's right to the kingdom: "<hi type="italic">It was his from the Lord.</hi> I was foolish in offering to contest it; and now that it is turned about to him I am satisfied." Thus he pretends to be well pleased with Solomon's accession to the throne, when he is doing all he can to give him disturbance. <hi type="italic">His words were smoother than butter, but war was in his heart.</hi> <div eID="gen6540" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6541" type="x-p"/> 3. Bathsheba's address to Solomon on his behalf. She promised to speak to the king for him (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.2.18">v. 18</reference>) and did so, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.2.19">v. 19</reference>. Solomon received her with all the respect that was due to a mother, though he himself was a king: He <hi type="italic">rose up to meet her, bowed himself to her,</hi> and caused her <hi type="italic">to sit on his right hand,</hi> according to the law of the fifth commandment. Children, not only when grown up, but when grown great, must give honour to their parents, and behave dutifully and respectfully towards them. <hi type="italic">Despise not thy mother when she is old.</hi> As a further instance of the deference he paid to his mother's wisdom and authority, when he understood she had a petition to present to him, he promised not to say her nay, a promise which both he and she understood with this necessary limitation, provided it be just and reasonable and fit to be granted; but, if it were otherwise, he was sure he should convince her that it was so, and that then she would withdraw it. She tells him her errand at last (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.2.21">v. 21</reference>): <hi type="italic">Let Abishag be given to Adonijah thy brother.</hi> It was strange that she did not suspect the treason, but more strange that she did not abhor the incest, that was in the proposal. But either she did not take Abishag to be David's wife, because the marriage was not consummated, or she thought it might be dispensed with to gratify Adonijah, in consideration of his tame submission to Solomon. This was her weakness and folly: it was well that she was not regent. Note, Those that have the ear of princes and great men, as it is their wisdom not to be too prodigal of their interest, so it is their duty never to use it for the assistance of sin or the furtherance of any wicked design. Let not princes be asked that which they ought not to grant. It ill becomes a good man to prefer a bad request or appear in a bad cause. <div eID="gen6541" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6542" type="x-p"/> 4. Solomon's just and judicious rejection of the request. Though his mother herself was the advocate, and called it <hi type="italic">a small petition,</hi> and perhaps it was the first she had troubled him with since he was king, yet he denied it, without violation of the general promise he had made, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.2.20">v. 20</reference>. If Herod had not had a mind to cut off John Baptist's head, he would not have thought himself obliged to do it by a general promise, like this, made to Herodias. The best friend we have in the world must not have such an interest in us as to bring us to do a wrong thing, either unjust or unwise. (1.) Solomon convinces his mother of the unreasonableness of the request, and shows her the tendency of it, which, before, she was not aware of. His reply is somewhat sharp: "<hi type="italic">Ask for him the kingdom also,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Kgs.2.22">v. 22</reference>. To ask that he may succeed the king in his bed is, in effect, to ask that he may succeed him in his throne; for that is it he aims at." Probably he had information, or cause for a strong suspicion, that Adonijah was plotting with Joab and Abiathar to give him disturbance, which warranted him to put this construction upon Adonijah's request. (2.) He convicts and condemns Adonijah for his pretensions, and both with an oath. He convicts him out of his own mouth, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.2.23">v. 23</reference>. His own tongue shall fall upon him; and a heavier load a man needs not fall under. Bathsheba may be imposed upon, but Solomon cannot; he plainly sees what Adonijah aims at, and concludes, "He has <hi type="italic">spoken this word against his own life;</hi> he is snared in the words of his own lips; now he shows what he would be at." He condemns him to die immediately: <hi type="italic">He shall be put to death this day,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Kgs.2.24">v. 24</reference>. God had himself declared with an oath that he would establish David's throne (<reference osisRef="Ps.89.35">Ps. lxxxix. 35</reference>), and therefore Solomon pledges the same assurance to secure that establishment, by cutting off the enemies of it. "As God liveth, that establisheth the government, Adonijah shall die, that would unsettle it." Thus the ruin of the enemies of Christ's kingdom is as sure as the stability of his kingdom, and both are as sure as the being and life of God, the founder of it. The warrant is immediately signed for his execution, and no less a man than Benaiah, the son of Jehoiada, general of the army, is ordered to be the executioner, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.2.25">v. 25</reference>. It is strange that Adonijah may not be heard to speak for himself: but Solomon's wisdom did not see it needful to examine the matter any further; it was plain enough that Adonijah aimed at the crown, and Solomon could not be safe while he lived. Ambitious turbulent spirits commonly prepare for themselves the instruments of death. Many a head has been lost by catching at a crown.
entries.ed4cf70d8cdd4d891b9f7646a8256f3bbd485da8: <div eID="gen6542" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Joab Put to Death. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1015.)</title> <div sID="gen6543" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">26</hi> And unto Abiathar the priest said the king, Get thee to Anathoth, unto thine own fields; for thou <hi type="italic">art</hi> worthy of death: but I will not at this time put thee to death, because thou barest the ark of the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> before David my father, and because thou hast been afflicted in all wherein my father was afflicted. <hi type="super">27</hi> So Solomon thrust out Abiathar from being priest unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; that he might fulfil the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , which he spake concerning the house of Eli in Shiloh. <hi type="super">28</hi> Then tidings came to Joab: for Joab had turned after Adonijah, though he turned not after Absalom. And Joab fled unto the tabernacle of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and caught hold on the horns of the altar. <hi type="super">29</hi> And it was told king Solomon that Joab was fled unto the tabernacle of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; and, behold, <hi type="italic">he is</hi> by the altar. Then Solomon sent Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, saying, Go, fall upon him. <hi type="super">30</hi> And Benaiah came to the tabernacle of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and said unto him, Thus saith the king, Come forth. And he said, Nay; but I will die here. And Benaiah brought the king word again, saying, Thus said Joab, and thus he answered me. <hi type="super">31</hi> And the king said unto him, Do as he hath said, and fall upon him, and bury him; that thou mayest take away the innocent blood, which Joab shed, from me, and from the house of my father. <hi type="super">32</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> shall return his blood upon his own head, who fell upon two men more righteous and better than he, and slew them with the sword, my father David not knowing <hi type="italic">thereof, to wit,</hi> Abner the son of Ner, captain of the host of Israel, and Amasa the son of Jether, captain of the host of Judah. <hi type="super">33</hi> Their blood shall therefore return upon the head of Joab, and upon the head of his seed for ever: but upon David, and upon his seed, and upon his house, and upon his throne, shall there be peace for ever from the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">34</hi> So Benaiah the son of Jehoiada went up, and fell upon him, and slew him: and he was buried in his own house in the wilderness. <div eID="gen6543" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6544" type="x-p"/> Abiathar and Joab were both aiding and abetting in Adonijah's rebellious attempt, and it is probable were at the bottom of this new motion made of Adonijah for Abishag, and it should seem Solomon knew it, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.2.22">v. 22</reference>. This was, in both, an intolerable affront both to God and to the government, and the worse because of their high station and the great influence their examples might have upon many. They therefore come next to be reckoned with. They are both equally guilty of the treason, but, in the judgment passed upon them, a difference is made and with good reason. <div eID="gen6544" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6545" type="x-p"/> I. Abiathar, in consideration of his old services, is only degraded, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.2.26-1Kgs.2.27">v. 26, 27</reference>. 1. Solomon convicts him, and by his great wisdom finds him guilty: "<hi type="italic">Thou art worthy of death,</hi> for joining with Adonijah, when thou knewest on whose head God intended to set the crown." 2. He calls to mind the respect he had formerly shown to David his father, and that he had both ministered to him in holy things (<hi type="italic">had borne before him the ark of the Lord</hi>), and also had tenderly sympathized with him in his afflictions and been afflicted in them all, particularly when he was in exile and distress both by Saul's persecution and Absalom's rebellion. Note, Those that show kindness to God's people shall have it remembered to their advantage one time or other. 3. For this reason he spares Abiathar's life, but deposes him from his offices, and confines him to his country seat at Anathoth, forbids him the court, the city, the tabernacle, the altar, and all inter-meddling in public business, with an intimation likewise that he was upon his good behaviour, and that though Solomon did not put him to death at this time he might another time, if he did not conduct himself well. But, for the present, he was only thrust out from being priest, as rendered unworthy that high station by the opposition he had given to that which he knew to be the will of God. Saul, for a supposed crime, had barbarously slain Abiathar's father, and eighty-five priests, their families, and city. Solomon spares Abiathar himself, though guilty of a real crime. Thus was Saul's government ruined and Solomon's established. As men are to God's ministers, they will find him to them. 4. The depriving of Abiathar was the fulfilling of the threatening against the house of Eli (<reference osisRef="1Sam.2.30">1 Sam. ii. 30</reference>), for he was the last high priest of that family. It was now above eighty years since the ruin was threatened; but God's judgments, though not executed speedily, will be executed surely. <div eID="gen6545" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6546" type="x-p"/> II. Joab, in consideration of his old sins, is put to death. <div eID="gen6546" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6547" type="x-p"/> 1. His guilty conscience sent him to the horns of the altar. He heard that Adonijah was executed and Abiathar deposed, and therefore, fearing his turn would be next, he fled for refuge to the altar. Many that, in the day of their security, care not for the service of the altar, will be glad of the protection of it in the day of their distress. Some think Joab designed thereby to devote himself for the future to a constant attendance upon the altar, hoping thereby to obtain his pardon, as some that have lived a dissolute life all their days have thought to atone for their crimes by retiring into a monastery when they are old, leaving the world when it has left them and no thanks to them. <div eID="gen6547" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6548" type="x-p"/> 2. Solomon ordered him to be put to death there for the murder of Abner and Amasa; for these were the crimes upon which he thought fit to ground the sentence, rather than upon his treasonable adherence to Adonijah. Joab was indeed worthy of death for turning after Adonijah, in contempt of Solomon and his designation to the throne, <hi type="italic">though he had not turned after Absalom,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Kgs.2.28">v. 28</reference>. Former fidelity will not serve to excuse any after treachery; yet, besides that, Joab had merited well of the house of David, to which and to his country he had done a great deal of good service in his day, in consideration of which, it is probable, Solomon would have pardoned him his offence against him (for clemency gives great reputation and establishment to an infant government), and would have only displaced him as he did Abiathar; but he must die for the murders he had formerly been guilty of, which his father had charged Solomon to call him to an account for. The debt he owed to the innocent blood that was shed, by answering its cries with the blood of him that shed, he could not pay himself, but left it to his son to pay it, who, having power wherewithal, failed not to do it. On this he grounds the sentence, aggravating the crime (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.2.32">v. 32</reference>), that he <hi type="italic">fell upon two men more righteous and better than he,</hi> that had done him no wrong nor meant him any, and, had they lived, might probably have done David better service (if the blood shed be not only innocent, but excellent, the life more valuable that common lives, the crime is the more heinous), that David knew not of it, and yet the case was such that he would be suspected as privy to it; so that Joab endangered his prince's reputation in taking away the life of his rivals, which was a further aggravation. For these crimes, (1.) He must die, and die by the sword of public justice. <hi type="italic">By man must his blood be shed,</hi> and it lies upon his own head (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.2.32">v. 32</reference>), as theirs does whom he had murdered, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.2.33">v. 33</reference>. Woe to the head that lies under the guilt of blood! Vengeance for murder was long in coming upon Joab; but, when it did come, it remained the longer, being here entailed <hi type="italic">upon the head of his seed for ever</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.2.33">v. 33</reference>), who, instead of deriving honour, as otherwise they might have done, from his heroic actions, derived guilt, and shame, and a curse, from his villainous actions, on account of which they fared the worse in this world. The seed of such evil doers shall never be renowned. (2.) He must die at the altar, rather than escape. Joab resolved not to stir from the altar (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.2.30">v. 30</reference>), hoping thereby either to secure himself or else to render Solomon odious to the people, as a profaner of the holy place, if he should put him to death there. Benaiah made a scruple of either killing him there or dragging him thence; but Solomon knew the law, that the altar of God should give no protection to wilful murderers. <reference osisRef="Exod.21.14">Exod. xxi. 14</reference>, <hi type="italic">Thou shalt take him from my altar that he may die,</hi> may die a sacrifice. In case of such sins as the blood of beasts would atone for the altar was a refuge, but not in Joab's case. He therefore orders him to be executed there, if he could not be got thence, to show that he feared not the censure of the people in doing his duty, but would rectify their mistake, and let them know that the administration of justice is better than sacrifice, and that the holiness of any place should never countenance the wickedness of any person. Those who, by a lively faith, take hold on Christ and his righteousness, with a resolution, if they perish, to perish there, shall find in him a more powerful protection than Joab found at the horns of the altar. Benaiah slew him (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.2.34">v. 34</reference>), with the solemnity, no doubt, of a public execution. The law being thus satisfied, he was <hi type="italic">buried in his own house in the wilderness,</hi> privately, like a criminal, not pompously, like a soldier; yet no indignity was done to his dead body. It is not for man to lay the iniquity upon the bones, whatever God does. <div eID="gen6548" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6549" type="x-p"/> 3. Solomon pleased himself with this act of justice, not as it gratified any personal revenge, but as it was the fulfilling of his father's orders and a real kindness to himself and his own government. (1.) Guilt was hereby removed, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.2.31">v. 31</reference>. By returning the innocent blood that had been shed upon the head of him that shed it, it was taken away from him and from the house of his father, which implies that the blood which is not required from the murderer will be required from the magistrate, at least there is danger lest it should. Those that would have their houses safe and built up must put away iniquity far from them. (2.) Peace was hereby secured (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.2.33">v. 33</reference>) upon David. He does not mean his person, but, as he explains himself in the next words, Upon <hi type="italic">his seed, his house, and his throne,</hi> shall there be <hi type="italic">peace for ever from the Lord;</hi> thus he expresses his desire that it may be so and his hope that it shall be so. "Now that justice is done, and the cry of blood is satisfied, the government will prosper." Thus <hi type="italic">righteousness and peace kiss each other.</hi> Now that such a turbulent man as Joab is removed there shall be peace. <hi type="italic">Take away the wicked from before the king, and his throne shall be established in righteousness,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.25.5">Prov. xxv. 5</reference>. Solomon, in this blessing of peace upon his house and throne, piously looks upward to God as the author of it. "It shall be peace from the Lord, and peace for ever from the Lord." The Lord of peace himself give us that peace which is everlasting.
entries.7ffc53fb7caa421ccb8b470516c98b8b06bc3d7d: <div eID="gen6549" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Shimei's Punishment. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1014.)</title> <div sID="gen6550" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">35</hi> And the king put Benaiah the son of Jehoiada in his room over the host: and Zadok the priest did the king put in the room of Abiathar. <hi type="super">36</hi> And the king sent and called for Shimei, and said unto him, Build thee a house in Jerusalem, and dwell there, and go not forth thence any whither. <hi type="super">37</hi> For it shall be, <hi type="italic">that</hi> on the day thou goest out, and passest over the brook Kidron, thou shalt know for certain that thou shalt surely die: thy blood shall be upon thine own head. <hi type="super">38</hi> And Shimei said unto the king, The saying <hi type="italic">is</hi> good: as my lord the king hath said, so will thy servant do. And Shimei dwelt in Jerusalem many days. <hi type="super">39</hi> And it came to pass at the end of three years, that two of the servants of Shimei ran away unto Achish son of Maachah king of Gath. And they told Shimei, saying, Behold, thy servants <hi type="italic">be</hi> in Gath. <hi type="super">40</hi> And Shimei arose, and saddled his ass, and went to Gath to Achish to seek his servants: and Shimei went, and brought his servants from Gath. <hi type="super">41</hi> And it was told Solomon that Shimei had gone from Jerusalem to Gath, and was come again. <hi type="super">42</hi> And the king sent and called for Shimei, and said unto him, Did I not make thee to swear by the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and protested unto thee, saying, Know for a certain, on the day thou goest out, and walkest abroad any whither, that thou shalt surely die? and thou saidst unto me, The word <hi type="italic">that</hi> I have heard <hi type="italic">is</hi> good. <hi type="super">43</hi> Why then hast thou not kept the oath of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and the commandment that I have charged thee with? <hi type="super">44</hi> The king said moreover to Shimei, Thou knowest all the wickedness which thine heart is privy to, that thou didst to David my father: therefore the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> shall return thy wickedness upon thine own head; <hi type="super">45</hi> And king Solomon <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> blessed, and the throne of David shall be established before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> for ever. <hi type="super">46</hi> So the king commanded Benaiah the son of Jehoiada; which went out, and fell upon him, that he died. And the kingdom was established in the hand of Solomon. <div eID="gen6550" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6551" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. The preferment of Benaiah and Zadok, two faithful friends to Solomon and his government, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.2.35">v. 35</reference>. Joab being put to death, Benaiah was advanced to be general of the forces in his room, and, Abiathar being deposed, Zadok was made high priest in his room, and therein was fulfilled the word of God, when he threatened to cut off the house of Eli (<reference osisRef="1Sam.2.35">1 Sam. ii. 35</reference>), <hi type="italic">I will raise me up a faithful priest, and will build him a sure house.</hi> Though sacred offices may be disgraced, they shall not be destroyed, by the mal-administration of those that are entrusted with them, nor shall God's work ever stand still for want of hands to carry it on. No wonder that he who was a king so immediately of God's making was empowered to make whom he though fit high priest; and he exercised this power with equity, for the ancient right was in Zadok, he being of the family of Eleazar, whereas Eli and his house were of Ithamar. <div eID="gen6551" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6552" type="x-p"/> II. The course that was taken with Shimei. He is sent for, by a messenger, from his house at Bahurim, expecting perhaps no better than Adonijah's doom, being conscious of his enmity to the house of David; but Solomon knows how to make a difference of crimes and criminals. David had promised Shimei his life for his time. Solomon is not bound by that promise, yet he will not go directly contrary to it. 1. He confines him to Jerusalem, and forbids him, upon any pretence whatsoever, to go out of the city any further than the brook Kidron, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.2.36-1Kgs.2.37">v. 36, 37</reference>. He would suffer him to continue at his country seat lest he should make mischief among his neighbours, but took him to Jerusalem, where he kept him prisoner at large. This might make Shimei's confinement easy to himself, for Jerusalem was beautiful for situation, <hi type="italic">the joy of the whole earth,</hi> the royal city, the holy city (he had no reason to complain of being shut up in such a paradise); it would also make it the more safe for Solomon, for there he would have him under his eye and be able to watch his motions; and he plainly tells him that if he ever go out of the rules he shall certainly die for it. This was a fair trial of his obedience, and such a test of his loyalty as he had no reason to complain of. He has his life upon easy terms: he shall live if he will but be content to live at Jerusalem. 2. Shimei submits to the confinement, and thankfully takes his life upon those terms. He enters into recognizance (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.2.38">v. 38</reference>), under the penalty of death, not to stir out of Jerusalem, and owns that the saying is good. Even those that perish cannot but own the conditions of pardon and life unexceptionable, so that their blood, like Shimei's, must rest upon their own heads. Shimei promised, with an oath, to keep within his bounds, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.2.42">v. 42</reference>. 3. Shimei forfeits his recognizance, which was the thing Solomon expected; and God was righteous in suffering him to do it, that he might now suffer for his old sins. Two of his servants (it seems, though he was a prisoner, he lived like himself, well attended) ran from him to the land of the Philistines, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.2.39">v. 39</reference>. Thither he pursued them, and thence brought them back to Jerusalem, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.2.40">v. 40</reference>. For the keeping of it private he <hi type="italic">saddled his ass</hi> himself, probably went in the night, and came home he thought undiscovered. "Seeking his servants," says bishop Hall, "he lost himself; those earthly things either are, or should be, our servants. How commonly do we see men run out of the bounds set by God's law, to hunt after them, till their souls incur a fearful judgment!" 4. Solomon takes the forfeiture. Information is given him that Shimei has transgressed, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.2.41">v. 41</reference>. The king sends for him, and, (1.) charges him with the present crime (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.2.42-1Kgs.2.43">v. 42, 43</reference>), that he had put a great contempt upon the authority and wrath both of God and the king, that he had broken <hi type="italic">the oath of the Lord</hi> and disobeyed the commandment of his prince, and by this it appeared what manner of spirit he was of, that he would not be held by the bonds of gratitude or conscience. Had he represented to Solomon the urgency of the occasion, and begged leave to go, perhaps Solomon might have given him leave; but to presume either upon his ignorance or his connivance was to affront him in the highest degree. (2.) He condemns him for his former crime, cursing David, and throwing stones at him in the day of his affliction: <hi type="italic">The wickedness which thy heart is privy to,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Kgs.2.44">v. 44</reference>. There was no need to examine witnesses for the proof of the fact, his own conscience was instead of a thousand witnesses. That wickedness which men's <hi type="italic">own hearts</hi> alone <hi type="italic">are privy to</hi> is enough, if duly considered, to fill them with confusion, in expectation of its return upon <hi type="italic">their own heads;</hi> for if the heart be privy to it, God is greater than the heart and knoweth all things. Others knew of Shimei's cursing David, but Shimei himself knew of the wicked principles of hatred and malice against David which he displayed in cursing him and that his submission was but feigned and forced. (3.) He blessed himself and his government (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.2.45">v. 45.</reference>): <hi type="italic">King Solomon shall be blessed,</hi> notwithstanding Shimei's impotent curses, which perhaps, in fury and despair, he now vented freely: <hi type="italic">Let them curse, but bless thou.</hi> And <hi type="italic">the throne of David shall be established,</hi> by taking away those that would undermine it. It is a comfort, in reference to the enmity of the church's enemies, that, how much soever they rage, it is a vain thing they imagine. Christ's throne is established, and they cannot shake it. (4.) He gives orders for the execution of Shimei immediately, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.2.46">v. 46</reference>. All judgment is committed to the Lord Jesus, and, though he be King of peace, he will be found a King of righteousness; and this will shortly be his word of command concerning all his enemies, that would not have him to reign over them: <hi type="italic">Bring them forth, and slay them before me;</hi> the reproaches of those that blasphemed him will fall on themselves, to their eternal condemnation.  <chapter eID="1Kgs.2"/> <div eID="gen6552" type="x-p"/>

entries.f761bb82bd452504fd3fc02334f174ef67ce1ad1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3083"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 2</title> <div sID="gen4282" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Kgs.2.1-1Kgs.2.11">1Ki 2:1-11</reference>. David Dies.<div eID="gen4282" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4283" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3083"/><hi type="bold">1. David ... charged Solomon his son--</hi>The charge recorded here was given to Solomon just before his death and is different from the farewell address delivered in public some time before (<reference osisRef="1Chr.28.2-1Chr.28.9">1Ch 28:2-9</reference>). It is introduced with great solemnity. <div eID="gen4283" type="x-p"/>
entries.92717f423e15de1e73e21366f90bf326028b5c11: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3084"/><div sID="gen4284" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3084"/><hi type="bold">2. I go the way of all the earth--</hi>a beautiful and impressive periphrasis for death.<div eID="gen4284" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4285" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">be thou strong, ... show thyself a man--</hi>This counsel is similar to the apostolic direction (<reference osisRef="1Cor.16.13">1Co 16:13</reference>) and refers to the fortitude or strength of mind that was required to discharge the onerous functions of king. <div eID="gen4285" type="x-p"/>
entries.9e8acff6f30e218fc9d8724566e95563137f06a6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3085"/><div sID="gen4286" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3085"/><hi type="bold">3. keep the charge of the Lord thy God--</hi>that is, the divine law in all its ceremonial as well as moral requirements. But particular reference was intended to its political institutions, as it was only by strictly maintaining the conduct that became the Hebrew monarch (<reference osisRef="Deut.17.10-Deut.17.20">De 17:10-20</reference>), that he would secure the blessing of peace and prosperity to his reign (see on <reference osisRef="Deut.4.5">De 4:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.29.10">De 29:10</reference>). <div eID="gen4286" type="x-p"/>
entries.934ee2296e06199be89f626d27df6d4d8628e684: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3086"/><div sID="gen4287" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3086"/><hi type="bold">4. there shall not fail thee ... a man on the throne of Israel--</hi>a reference to the promise made to David of the sovereignty being vested perpetually in his lineage (<reference osisRef="2Sam.7.11-2Sam.7.16">2Sa 7:11-16</reference>), which was confirmed to Solomon afterwards (see <reference osisRef="1Kgs.9.5">1Ki 9:5</reference>), and repeated with reference to its spiritual meaning long after (<reference osisRef="Jer.33.17">Jr 33:17</reference>). <div eID="gen4287" type="x-p"/>
entries.c5f0128634715d9e605f992fb830ffa156ab61ac: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3087"/><div sID="gen4288" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3087"/><hi type="bold">5-6. thou knowest also what Joab ... did--</hi>The insolent and imperious conduct of that general had not only been deeply offensive to the feelings (<reference osisRef="2Sam.18.5-2Sam.15.19">2Sa 18:5-15; 19</reference>:<reference osisRef="2Sam.15.5-2Sam.15.7">5-7</reference>), but calculated to bring reproach on the character, to injure the prospects, and endanger the throne of David. Passing over the injuries committed directly against himself, David dwelt with strong feelings on the base assassination of Abner and Amasa.<div eID="gen4288" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4289" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shed the blood of war in peace, &c.--</hi>The obvious meaning is, that in peace he acted towards them as if they had been in a state of warfare; but perhaps these graphic expressions might be designed to impress Solomon's mind more strongly with a sense of the malice, treachery, and cruelty by which those murders were characterized. <div eID="gen4289" type="x-p"/>
entries.92382edd097143d51fa84f984a6409bb5f36346b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3089"/><div sID="gen4291" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3089"/><hi type="bold">8. thou hast with thee Shimei--</hi>Though David promised him a pardon, which being enforced by the presence of a thousand followers, could not have been well refused, he warned his son against Shimei as a turbulent and dangerous character. It must not be supposed that in these dying instructions David was evincing a fierce, vindictive spirit. He is rather to be considered as acting in the character of a king and magistrate, in noticing crimes which he had not been in a condition to punish, and pointing out persons of whom Solomon would be under a necessity to rid himself as dangerous to the state. The grateful mention of Barzillai's kindness [1Ki 2:7] was, however, a personal feeling that does honor to the warmth of his heart; and his silence as to Mephibosheth, the son of his beloved Jonathan, would imply the previous death of that prince. <div eID="gen4291" type="x-p"/>
entries.3b4c74e8a373b8e35193f8ae929f44275dc9c4b7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3090"/><div sID="gen4292" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3090"/><hi type="bold">9. for thou art a wise man--</hi>Solomon had given early indications of wisdom before his miraculous endowment with the heavenly gift (see <reference osisRef="1Kgs.3.11">1Ki 3:11</reference>), and his own sagacity would dictate the course that should be followed in any new offense that Shimei might commit. <div eID="gen4292" type="x-p"/>
entries.6d31926162d225a1234c54ae2b489eb4220dda9d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3091"/><div sID="gen4293" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3091"/><hi type="bold">10. So David slept with his fathers--</hi>about six months after the coronation of Solomon (compare <reference osisRef="2Sam.5.5">2Sa 5:5</reference> with <reference osisRef="1Chr.29.27">1Ch 29:27</reference>). The interval was spent in developing his ideas and plans for the future glory of the kingdom and providing for the permanent worship of God (see on <reference osisRef="1Chr.22.1">1Ch 22:1</reference>, and following).<div eID="gen4293" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4294" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">was buried in the city of David--</hi>Sepulchres were not allowed within the precincts of cities. Jerusalem, however, formed an exception; and yet, even there, the privilege was reserved chiefly for the royal family (<reference osisRef="Acts.2.29">Ac 2:29</reference>). Tradition says that the bones of David repose on Mount Zion, and the minaret of a small mosque points out the spot which tradition has fixed. His was a noble, a wondrous, and a humbling history. He was a good man, yet his life was deformed by various crimes of a very gross character. But there were many bright and noble traits in his character; he was an earnest lover of the divine law; his reign was signalized by many important services that contributed to the glory of God and the exaltation of His kingdom; and his name, as the sweet Psalmist of Israel, will be held in honor to the latest age of the Church.<div eID="gen4294" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4295" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Kgs.2.12-1Kgs.2.24">1Ki 2:12-24</reference>. Solomon Succeeds Him. <div eID="gen4295" type="x-p"/>
entries.b679179ee16dfea14b626fbe346a5aeb136aca85: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3092"/><div sID="gen4296" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3092"/><hi type="bold">12. Then sat Solomon upon the throne of David his father--</hi>His ascension to the royal dignity was made under the happiest auspices. Having been born after his father became monarch of the whole kingdom, his claim, according to the notions of Oriental people, was preferable to that of all, even his elder brothers. The Hebrew kingdom enjoyed internal prosperity; it was respected and renowned abroad, and Solomon well knew how to improve these advantages. <div eID="gen4296" type="x-p"/>
entries.ef5c14907a7c55da382dd677471c026beb9fd238: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3093"/><div sID="gen4297" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3093"/><hi type="bold">13-18. Adonijah ... came to Bath-sheba--</hi>Her question to him betrays an apprehension which his recent conduct might well warrant; but his pious acknowledgment of the divine will seemed apparently to indicate so entire an acquiescence in the settlement of the succession [1Ki 2:15], that, in her womanly simplicity, she perceived not the deep cunning and evil design that was concealed under his request and readily undertook to promote his wishes. <div eID="gen4297" type="x-p"/>
entries.f6ec93a6d4bce7ed5b2372ec23a42150fc211a16: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3094"/><div sID="gen4298" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3094"/><hi type="bold">19-20. Bath-sheba ... went unto King Solomon--</hi>The filial reverence and the particular act of respect, which Solomon rendered, were quite in accordance with the sentiments and customs of the East. The right hand is the place of honor; and as it expressly said to have been assigned to "the king's mother," it is necessary to remark that, when a husband dies, his widow acquires a higher dignity and power, as a mother over her son, than she ever possessed before. Besides, the dignity of "king's mother" is a state office, to which certain revenues are attached. The holder has a separate palace or court, as well as possesses great influence in public affairs; and as the dignity is held for life, it sometimes happens, in consequence of deaths, that the person enjoying it may not be related to the reigning sovereign by natural maternity. Bath-sheba had evidently been invested with this honorable office. <div eID="gen4298" type="x-p"/>
entries.3f8dbd1baa9e8b937676f4f3815d64ec83d84d7e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3095"/><div sID="gen4299" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3095"/><hi type="bold">22. why dost thou ask Abishag ... ask for him the kingdom also--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="2Sam.16.5">2Sa 16:5</reference>; also see on <reference osisRef="2Sam.12.8">2Sa 12:8</reference>). Solomon's indignation was roused; he in a moment penetrated the artful scheme, and from his associating the names of Abiathar and Joab, he seems to have suspected or known that those deep schemers had been the prompters of Adonijah. <div eID="gen4299" type="x-p"/>
entries.0d91b81a9a7416b91f86f676867854e09ea3074f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3096"/><div sID="gen4300" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3096"/><hi type="bold">23-25. God do so to me, and more also--</hi>the common form of introducing a solemn oath.<div eID="gen4300" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4301" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">if Adonijah have not spoken this word against his own life--</hi>Whether there was a treasonable design to conceal under this request or not, the act, according to Eastern notions, was criminal, and of dangerous consequence to the state. There is no ground of censure upon Solomon for cruelty or precipitation in this instance. He had pardoned Adonijah's former conspiracy; but this new attempt was rebellion against the viceroy appointed by the divine King and called for condign punishment. The office of executioner was among the Hebrews, as in other ancient countries of the East, performed unceremoniously and privately--often without any previous warning--by the captain of the guard, or one of his officers (<reference osisRef="Matt.14.10">Mt 14:10</reference>). <div eID="gen4301" type="x-p"/>
entries.c6e7c951be00cca19d964f9c9c3423709a3cbb39: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3097"/><div sID="gen4302" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3097"/><hi type="bold">26-27. unto Abiathar the priest said the king--</hi>This functionary, as the counsellor or accomplice of Adonijah, had deserved to share his fate. But partly from regard to his priestly dignity, and partly from his long associations with the late king, Solomon pronounced on him the mitigated sentence of banishment to his country estate at Anathoth, and thereby, as God's vicegerent, deprived him of his office and its emoluments. The sacred writer notices the remarkable fulfilment, Abiathar's degradation from the high priesthood (see on <reference osisRef="1Kgs.4.4">1Ki 4:4</reference>), of the doom denounced against the house of Eli (<reference osisRef="1Sam.2.30">1Sa 2:30</reference>).<div eID="gen4302" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4303" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Kgs.2.28-1Kgs.2.45">1Ki 2:28-45</reference>. Joab Slain. <div eID="gen4303" type="x-p"/>
entries.fcc04298991132b9a1dd3807e3db65f174e3c87d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3098"/><div sID="gen4304" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3098"/><hi type="bold">28. Then tidings came to Joab--</hi>The execution of these sentences respectively on Adonijah and Abiathar prepared Joab for his fate. Death, due to his great crimes (<reference osisRef="Num.35.33">Nu 35:33</reference>), would long ago have been inflicted, had not his power and popularity with the army been too formidable for the old king. He now fled to the altar, which, though a recognized asylum, afforded no sanctuary to the rebel and murderer (<reference osisRef="Exod.21.14">Ex 21:14</reference>). And, as he refused to leave it, he seems to have cherished some faint hope that a religious scruple would have been felt at the thought of violating the sanctity of the place by bloodshed. Benaiah, not liking to assume any responsibility, referred the matter to Solomon, who determined that the law should take its course (<reference osisRef="Deut.19.13">De 19:13</reference>). <div eID="gen4304" type="x-p"/>
entries.1fe2b2b0ce25075981beb5ff192a13bef6c5c3ba: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3099"/><div sID="gen4305" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3099"/><hi type="bold">33. Their blood shall ... return upon the head of Joab, &c.--</hi>A reference is here made to the curse publicly and solemnly pronounced by King David (<reference osisRef="2Sam.3.28">2Sa 3:28</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Sam.3.29">29</reference>).<div eID="gen4305" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4306" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Kgs.2.34-1Kgs.2.46">1Ki 2:34-46</reference>. Shimei Put to Death. <div eID="gen4306" type="x-p"/>
entries.288214ac375102a4f107b9bf45103ce867662fbd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3100"/><div sID="gen4307" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3100"/><hi type="bold">34. Benaiah ... went up, and fell upon him--</hi>According to the terms of the statute (<reference osisRef="Exod.21.14">Ex 21:14</reference>), and the practice in similar cases (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.11.15">2Ki 11:15</reference>), the criminal was to be dragged from the altar and slain elsewhere. But the truth is, that the sanctity of the altar was violated as much by the violence used in forcing the criminal from the place as in shedding his blood there; the express command of God authorized the former and therefore by implication permitted the latter.<div eID="gen4307" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4308" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">was buried in his own house--</hi>or family vault, at his property in the wilderness of Judah. His interment was included in the king's order, as enjoined in the divine law (<reference osisRef="Deut.21.23">De 21:23</reference>). <div eID="gen4308" type="x-p"/>
entries.a20a9691c2f05f0b092f559c7b81ac3bdd8547b4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3101"/><div sID="gen4309" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3101"/><hi type="bold">36. the king sent and called for Shimei--</hi>He was probably residing at Bahurim, his native place. But, as he was a suspicious character, Solomon condemned him henceforth to live in Jerusalem, on the penalty of death, for going without the gates. He submitted to this confinement for three years, when, violating his oath, he was arrested and put to death by Solomon for perjury, aggravated by his former crime of high treason against David [1Ki 2:42-44]. <div eID="gen4309" type="x-p"/>
entries.8a391ba0bd2952ab3cc47594aec48d9bbf1f3520: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3102"/><div sID="gen4310" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3102"/><hi type="bold">46. the kingdom was established in the hand of Solomon--</hi>Now, by the death of Shimei, all the leaders of the rival factions had been cut off. <chapter eID="1Kgs.2"/>

entries.540043144848713846585c0245874e7445f6bea4: <div eID="gen11479" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen11480" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen11481" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen11481" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen11480" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen11482" type="x-p"/> David leaves his dying charge with Solomon, relative to his own personal conduct, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.2.1-1Kgs.2.4">1Kgs 2:1-4</reference>; to Joab, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.2.5">1Kgs 2:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.2.6">1Kgs 2:6</reference>; to Barzillai, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.2.7">1Kgs 2:7</reference>; to Shimei, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.2.8">1Kgs 2:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.2.9">1Kgs 2:9</reference>. He dies, and Solomon is established in the kingdom, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.2.10-1Kgs.2.12">1Kgs 2:10-12</reference>. Adonijah requests to have Abishag to wife, and is put to death by Solomon, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.2.13-1Kgs.2.25">1Kgs 2:13-25</reference>. Abiathar the priest is banished to his estate at Anathoth, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.2.26">1Kgs 2:26</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.2.27">1Kgs 2:27</reference>. Joab, fearing for his life, flees to the horns of the altar, and is slain there by Benaiah, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.2.28-1Kgs.2.34">1Kgs 2:28-34</reference>. Benaiah is made captain of the host in his stead, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.2.35">1Kgs 2:35</reference>. Shimei is ordered to confine himself to Jerusalem, and never leave it on pain of death, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.2.36-1Kgs.2.38">1Kgs 2:36-38</reference>. After three years he follows some of his runaway servants to Gath, and thereby forfeits his life, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.2.39">1Kgs 2:39</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.2.40">1Kgs 2:40</reference>. Solomon sends for him, upbraids him, and commands him to be slain by Benaiah, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.2.41-1Kgs.2.46">1Kgs 2:41-46</reference>.
entries.818ac6988d3060068828d3c52dc2bd561a66a3dc: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen11482" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11483" type="x-p"/> I go the way of all the earth - I am dying. All the inhabitants of the earth must come to the dust. In life, some follow one occupation, some another; but all must, sooner or later, come to the grave. Death is no respecter of persons; he visits the palace of the king as well as the cottage of the peasant. <div eID="gen11483" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11484" type="x-p"/> Pallida mors aequo pulsat pede pauperum tabernas, <div eID="gen11484" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11485" type="x-p"/> Regumque turres. - <div eID="gen11485" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11486" type="x-p"/> Hor. Odar. lib. i., od. iv., ver. 13. "With equal pace, impartial fate <div eID="gen11486" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11487" type="x-p"/> Knocks at the palace as the cottage gate." <div eID="gen11487" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11488" type="x-p"/> Francis. - Sed omnes una manet nox, <div eID="gen11488" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11489" type="x-p"/> Et calcanda semel via lethi. - <div eID="gen11489" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11490" type="x-p"/> Ib. od. xxviii., ver. 15. "One dreary night for all mankind remains, <div eID="gen11490" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11491" type="x-p"/> And once we all must tread the shadowy plains." <div eID="gen11491" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11492" type="x-p"/> Ibid. <div eID="gen11492" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11493" type="x-p"/> There is no respect to age or youth more than to station or external circumstance: - <div eID="gen11493" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11494" type="x-p"/> Mixta senum ac juvenum densantur funera: nullum <div eID="gen11494" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11495" type="x-p"/> Saeva caput Proserpina fugit. <div eID="gen11495" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11496" type="x-p"/> Ib. od. xxviii., ver. 19. <div eID="gen11496" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11497" type="x-p"/> Thus age and youth promiscuous crowd the tomb; <div eID="gen11497" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11498" type="x-p"/> No mortal head can shun the impending doom." <div eID="gen11498" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11499" type="x-p"/> Ibid. <div eID="gen11499" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11500" type="x-p"/> And it is not merely man that is subjected to this necessity; all that have in them the breath of life must lose it; it is the way of all the earth, both of men and inferior animals. - Terrestria quando Mortales animas vivunt sortita, neque ulla est Aut parvo aut magno lethi fuga. <div eID="gen11500" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11501" type="x-p"/> Vive memor quam sis aevi brevis. <div eID="gen11501" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11502" type="x-p"/> Hor. Sat. l. ii., s. vi., ver. 93. "All that tread the earth are subject to mortality; neither great nor small can avoid death. <div eID="gen11502" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11503" type="x-p"/> Live therefore conscious that your time is short." <div eID="gen11503" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11504" type="x-p"/> It is painful to the pride of the great and mighty that, however decorated their tombs may be, they must undergo the same dissolution and corruption with the vulgar dead; for the grave is the house appointed for all living: man is born to die. <div eID="gen11504" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11505" type="x-p"/> Omnium idem exitus est, sed et idem domicilium. "For all have the same end, and are huddled together in the same narrow house." <div eID="gen11505" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11506" type="x-p"/> Here emperors, kings, statesmen, warriors, heroes, and butchers of all kinds, with peasants and beggars, meet; however various their routes, they terminate in the same point. This and all other kindred sentiments on the subject are well expressed in that excellent little poem of Mr. Blair, entitled "The Grave," which opens with the following lines: - <div eID="gen11506" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11507" type="x-p"/> While some affect the sun, and some the shade; Some flee the city, some the hermitage; Their aims as various as the roads they take In journeying through life; the task be mine To paint the gloomy horrors of the tomb, The appointed place of rendezvous, where all These travelers meet. <div eID="gen11507" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11508" type="x-p"/> Show thyself a man - Act like a rational being, and not like a brute; and remember, that he acts most like a man who is most devoted to his Good.
entries.24eb8c224b08a9e7bb1847edc205825cde1fc9e7: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen11508" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11509" type="x-p"/> Keep the charge of the Lord - Keep what God has given thee to keep. <div eID="gen11509" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11510" type="x-p"/> 1. Walk in his ways. Not in thine own, nor in the ways of a wicked, perishing world. <div eID="gen11510" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11511" type="x-p"/> 2. Keep his statutes. Consider all his appointments to be holy, just, and good; receive them as such, and conscientiously observe them. <div eID="gen11511" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11512" type="x-p"/> 3. Keep his commandments. Whatever he has bidden thee to do, perform; what he has forbidden thee to do, omit. <div eID="gen11512" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11513" type="x-p"/> 4. Keep his judgments. What he has determined to be right, is essentially and inherently right; what he has determined to be wrong or evil, is inherently and essentially so. A thing is not good because God has commanded it; a thing is not evil because he has forbidden it. He has commanded the good, because it is in its own nature good and useful; he has forbidden the evil, because it is in its own nature bad and hurtful. Keep therefore his judgments. <div eID="gen11513" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11514" type="x-p"/> 5. Keep his testimonies. Bear witness to all to which he has borne witness. His testimonies are true; there is no deceit or falsity in them. His testimonies refer also to future good things and good times; they are the significators of coming blessedness: as such, respect them. <div eID="gen11514" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11515" type="x-p"/> That thou mayest prosper - If thou hast God's approbation, thou wilt have God's blessing. If thy ways please him, he will not withhold from thee any manner of thing that is good.
entries.fb2fc93badf7f8ac53178e1a82a47353433c4413: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen11515" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11516" type="x-p"/> That the Lord may continue his word - The prosperity which God has promised to grant to my family will depend on their faithfulness to the good they receive; if they live to God, they shall sit for ever on the throne of Israel. But alas! they did not; and God's justice cut off the entail made by his mercy.
entries.d8c59c969f1bdb5f5bc122e326c88fabfb5ac0e7: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen11516" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11517" type="x-p"/> Thou knowest - what Joab - did to me - He did every thing bad and dishonorable in itself, in the murder of Abner and Amasa, and indeed in the death of the profligate Absalom. <div eID="gen11517" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11518" type="x-p"/> Shed the blood of war - upon his girdle - and in his shoes - He stabbed them while he pretended to embrace them, so that their blood gushed out on his girdle, and fell into his shoes! This was a most abominable aggravation of his crimes.
entries.2868f9edfa40e35c5efa8eae6c626018e9c26306: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen11518" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11519" type="x-p"/> Let not his hoar head go down to the grave in peace - It would have been an insult to justice not to have taken the life of Joab. David was culpable in delaying it so long; but probably the circumstances of his government would not admit of his doing it sooner. According to the law of God, Joab, having murdered Abner and Amasa, should die. And had not David commanded Solomon to perform this act of justice, he could not have died in the approbation of his Maker.
entries.6990d303bb269e393154dc1b0f203d937b37fc9e: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen11519" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11520" type="x-p"/> But show kindness unto the sons of Barzillai - See the notes on <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.31">2Sam 19:31</reference> (note), etc.
entries.5248ca28c70cd490bd3a55465b7a2b46c930b593: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen11520" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11521" type="x-p"/> Thou hast with thee Shimei - See on <reference osisRef="2Sam.16.5">2Sam 16:5</reference> (note), etc., and the notes on <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.18-2Sam.19.23">2Sam 19:18-23</reference> (note).
entries.819d95e56daf7a2d3f94cf3f7373ba95720f50fa: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen11521" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11522" type="x-p"/> Hold him not guiltless - Do not consider him as an innocent man, though I have sworn to him that I would not put him to death by the sword; yet as thou art a wise man, and knowest how to treat such persons, treat him as he deserves; only as I have sworn to him, and he is an aged man, let him not die a violent death; bring not down his hoary head to the grave with blood. So Solomon understood David, and so I think David should be understood; for the negative particle לא lo, in the former clause, hold him Not guiltless, should be repeated in this latter clause, though not expressed, his hoary head bring thou Not down; instances of which frequently occur in the Hebrew Bible. See Dr. Kennicott's note at the end of this chapter, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.2.46">1Kgs 2:46</reference> (note).
entries.ccb801ce4137187ab6cfd2ca797a3ce915b02ec0: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen11522" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11523" type="x-p"/> David slept with his fathers - His life was a life of remarkable providences, of much piety, and of great public usefulness. In general he lived well, and it is most evident that he died well; and as a king, a general, a poet, a father, and a friend, he has had few equals, and no superior, from his own time to the present day. But I shall reserve a more particular consideration of his character till I come to the book of Psalms, in which that character, with all its lights and shades, is exhibited by his own masterly hand. And it is from this composition alone that we can know David, and the maxims by which he was governed in public and private life. <div eID="gen11523" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11524" type="x-p"/> Was buried in the city of David - And Solomon, says Josephus, deposited immense treasures with him, in the grave, where they continued unmolested for thirteen hundred years, till Hyrcanus, the high priest, being besieged by Antiochus, opened the sepulcher, and took thence three thousand talents, part of which he gave to Antiochus, to raise the siege. It is added that, many years afterwards, Herod the Great ransacked this tomb and got considerable riches. Little credit is due to this account, though we know that was customary in ancient times to deposit with the more illustrious dead, gold, silver, and precious stones. That the tomb of David existed in the days of the apostles, we learn from <reference osisRef="Act.2.29">Act 2:29</reference>, where St. Peter, addressing the Jews, says, Men and brethren, let me speak freely to you of the patriarch David; that he is both dead and buried, and his sepulcher is with us unto this day. St. Jerome speaks of it as existing in his time, and modern travelers pretend that it is still in existence. But both monks and Mohammedans have long united to impose on Christian pilgrims; and there is scarcely any dependence to be placed on any of their relations; absurdity and self-contradiction are their principal characteristics.
entries.1d0afa1971043b8a15a23de31c14f6208d510170: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen11524" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11525" type="x-p"/> Thou knowest that the kingdom was mine - It certainly was his by the right of primogeniture, and it was his by the voice of the people, and the consent of the high priest.
